food.text: In 675 CE, Emperor Tenmu decreed a prohibition on eating cattle, horses, dogs, monkeys, and chickens during the 4th to 9th months of the year. To break the law would mean a death sentence. The decree was shaped by the influence of Chinese culture and Buddhism, which marked the taboos on meat in Japan. It did not ban deer or wild boar, which were important to the Japanese diet at that time.
Rice has been a staple of Japanese cuisine since early times, and wheat and soybeans were introduced shortly after it. All three remain staple foods in Japan today.

Emperor Tenmu's 675 ban did not cover deer or wild boar, the two most commonly eaten meats in Japan. This omission suggests that influences other than Buddhist morality helped shape the law. Tenmu was a well-known sponsor of Buddhism.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

food.text: Buddhism became widely accepted with the rise of the Soga clan, and a taboo on eating meat, especially mammals, became common practice. Even so, impoverished mountain people still hunted wild game. Townspeople would eat it when the opportunity arose.
Chopsticks were introduced to Japan during the Asuka period. At first only the nobility used them, while the general population ate with their hands because utensils were quite expensive.

In 752 CE, Empress Kōken decreed a ban on fishing, one of many decrees by emperors and empresses in the 8th century banning the killing of any animals. She promised that adequate rice would be given to fishermen whose livelihood would otherwise have been destroyed.
In 927 CE, regulations stated that any government official or noble who ate meat was deemed unclean for three days. Such a person could not take part in Shinto observances at the imperial court.

Emperor Tenmu's ban was strengthened by later rulers, including Empress Genshō in 721 and Emperor Shōmu in 736. The ban is mentioned in the Nihon Shoki. Even so, mentions of eating wild boar and deer persisted from the 8th century into the 16th century.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

food.text: Chickens had been introduced to Japan from China with the advent of rice farming. Chicken meat was prohibited under Emperor Tenmu's 675 edict, although birds such as pheasants and wild ducks were not.
food.source_title: History of meat consumption in Japan

food.text: In Japan, cattle and horses were rare and valued more for labor and transportation. A cow or horse would be ritually sacrificed on the first day of rice paddy cultivation, a ritual introduced from China.

Some regions kept eating meat despite the bans of the 8th and 9th centuries. In Kagoshima pig farming flourished, and in Oumi there was a culture of eating beef. In the Suwa region, deer were sacrificed in Shinto rituals.

art.text: The earliest Japanese sculptures of the Buddha date to the 6th and 7th century. They ultimately derive from the Greco-Buddhist art of Gandhara, with Chinese artistic traits superimposed on it.

The earliest complex art in Japan was produced in the 7th and 8th centuries in connection with Buddhism. In the 9th century, the Japanese began to turn away from China and develop indigenous forms of expression, and the secular arts became increasingly important.

Buddhist art and religious thought reached Japan from China by way of Korea. The Three Kingdoms, and particularly Baekje, were instrumental as active agents in introducing Buddhism to Japan in 538 or 552, so Korea was more than a mere transmitter.

Korean sculpture was exported to Japan, primarily during the Baekje period, and Korean Buddhist sculptures from the seventh century still exist there. Korean sculptures were generally made of wood, then later stone, and then ceramic.

Goguryeo tomb murals date from around AD 500 and still show strong colors. They depict daily life and Korean mythologies of the time. By 2005, 70 murals had been found, mostly in the Taedong river basin near Pyongyang.

Baekje was founded in 18 BC and built great temples after establishing friendships with China and Japan. Its earliest stone pagoda, at Mireuksa Temple in Iksan county, is of particular interest because it shows the transition from a wooden pagoda to a stone one.

The Takamatsuzuka Tomb in Japan dates from the 7th-century end of the Goguryeo period. Its paintings may show Goguryeo influence, having been made either by Goguryeo artists or by Japanese artists trained by Goguryeo people.

The earliest Japanese Buddha sculptures date to the 6th and 7th centuries. Their roots lie in the Greco-Buddhist art of Gandhara, with Chinese traits added, and the Kōryū-ji Miroku Bosatsu and the Chūgū-ji Siddhartha statues show this transmission.
Buddhist art in Japan was encouraged by Crown Prince Shōtoku in the Suiko period in the sixth century. Emperor Shōmu did the same in the Nara period in the eighth century.

The semi-seated Maitreya form was transmitted to Japan, as shown by the Kōryū-ji Miroku Bosatsu and the Chūgū-ji Siddhartha statues. These works show how a style with Greek roots travelled across Asia to reach Japan.

Nara period sculptors adopted the hollow-core dry lacquer technique, which may have been used to reduce the use of bronze. Sculpture also began to show deities and guardian figures with individualistic and expressive features, rather than only Buddhas and bodhisattvas.

The Triad of Yakushi at Yakushiji temple in Nara shows the healing Buddha attended by the bodhisattvas Nikko and Gakko. It reveals Chinese and central Asian influences in its anatomical definition, naturalism and realistic drapery.

The Murō-ji, from the early 9th century, is set deep in cypress trees on a mountain southeast of Nara and best reflects the spirit of early Heian Shingon temples. Its wooden Shakyamuni has a ponderous body, thick drapery folds carved in the honpa-shiki rolling-wave style, and an austere, withdrawn face.

In terms of painting, Nara period Buddhist works emulated the Chinese Tang style, which was characterized by elongated and rounded figures and broad brush strokes. The early Nara period also saw a move toward more naturalistic styles emerging from China.

war.text: On July 11, 645, a small but elite Tang army wiped out a Goguryeo relief force at the Battle of Mount Jupil, in what the article calls a one-sided mass slaughter. The Goguryeo troops had been sent to strengthen the defenses of the fortress city of Ansi. 30,000 of them were killed trying to break out of the encirclement, and the Tang won a major victory.
In 668, Silla conquered Baekje and Goguryeo with the aid of the Tang dynasty, forming Unified Silla. Balhae succeeded Goguryeo in the north. The peninsula's Three Kingdoms period thus ended.

Japan's centralization was greatly accelerated by a devastating defeat at the hands of the Chinese Tang dynasty in the Battle of Baekgang in the latter half of the 7th century. In response, domestic powers reached a consensus to build a national system, leading to a rapid consolidation of centralized power. The Taika Reform of the mid-7th century had achieved only some progress, and the Jinshin War of 672, a bloody conflict between Prince Ōama and his nephew Prince Ōtomo, two rivals to the throne, was a further catalyst for administrative reform.

The Later Three Kingdoms period (c. 890s to 936) was a partial revival of the old three kingdoms of early medieval Korea. Its start and end dates are loosely defined and differ across academic sources.

The Tang invasion of Goguryeo, decided on in 644 by Emperor Taizong of Tang, commenced on 1 April 645. The pretext was the murder of King Yeongnyu and other officials by the military dictator Yŏn Kaesomun, who killed them because they courted the Emperor of China and kept the kingdom on friendly terms with China, which he, a military hardliner, never approved. Li Shiji's forces crossed into Goguryeo that day.

Kyŏn Hwŏn captured Gwangju and established the state of Later Baekje at Jeonju in 892. He proclaimed Later Baekje a kingdom in 900. Historians use these events, or the first major rebellions against Unified Silla in 889, to mark the start of the Later Three Kingdoms.

In 918, Goguryeo was resurrected as Goryeo. Korean historians call its achievement a "true national unification", because it unified both the Later Three Kingdoms and the ruling class of Balhae after its fall.

Yŏn Kaesomun mobilized an army of 150,000 soldiers under generals Ko Hyejin and Ko Yŏnsu by June 645. The source calls this proportionately huge for a kingdom with a small population and a fragile economy.

Ansi was the capital of Yodong province, the second-largest city in Goguryeo with 100,000 inhabitants, and the center of its northern overland defenses. Tang forces reached its gates by 11 June 645. Had it fallen, the rest of Goguryeo south of the Yalu River would have been defenseless.
The Later Three Kingdoms ended in two steps. Gyeongsun, the last Silla monarch, surrendered to Goryeo in 935. Goryeo then conquered Later Baekje in 936.

After the battle, the Tang emperor began a siege of Ansi that lasted three months. Bad weather and dwindling supplies forced the besiegers to lift it, and the city was saved. Yet the destruction of the relief army, with tens of thousands of Goguryeo soldiers killed or captured, drained Goguryeo's limited manpower, and the kingdom fell in 668.

The two armies faced each other on the plain at the foot of Mount Jupil by 21 June 645. The Goguryeo army stood just across a river at the south end of the plain. The battle itself came on July 11, ending with the Goguryeo relief force encircled and slaughtered, 30,000 of its men killed in a failed breakout, 3,800 wounded and famished survivors on the mountain surrendering, and 33,000 captured, of whom 3,300 Mohe troops were executed.

literature.text: Chinese literature reached Japan around the 6th century CE, mostly by way of the Korean peninsula. Chinese historical writings, religious scriptures and poetry laid the foundation for Japanese literature proper. The source compares this influence to that of Latin on the European languages and literature.

The earliest literary works in Japan were created in the Nara period. They include the Kojiki of 712, a historical record that chronicles ancient mythology and folk songs, the Nihon Shoki of 720, and the poetry anthology Man'yōshū of 759. Together these works mark the beginning of Japan's written literary record.

Chinese characters were adapted in Japan to create man'yōgana, the earliest form of kana, or Japanese syllabic writing. During the Heian period, the significant use and development of kana let literature establish its own style. This was part of the growth of Japan's original kokufū culture.
Korea's hyangga, or native songs, were the first uniquely Korean form of poetry. They originally meant songs sung in the Silla period. Only twenty five survive.

The Man'yōshū preserves from the eighth century 265 chōka (long poems) and 4,207 tanka (short poems). It also holds one tan-renga, one bussokusekika, four kanshi (Chinese poems) and 22 Chinese prose passages. It shows how Japanese-language and Chinese-language writing sat side by side.

Kakinomoto no Hitomaro is described as the greatest poet of the early days and one of the most significant in the Man'yōshū. He and Nukata no Ōkimi were significant poets in its first three sections. Those sections contain mostly works from the middle of the 7th century to the early part of the 8th century.

Under the influence of Tang dynasty Chinese poets, Japanese began to compose poetry in Chinese, called kanshi. It took several hundred years to digest this foreign impact and merge kanshi into a Japanese-language literary tradition. Only then did native forms such as waka develop.

The tale of Urashima Tarō, first described in the Nihongi in 720, is an early example of proto-science fiction. A young fisherman named Urashima Taro visits an undersea palace and stays there for three days. When he returns to his village, he finds himself three hundred years in the future, where he is long forgotten, his house in ruins, and his family long dead.

The Nihon Shoki of 720 was a chronicle written in Chinese. It is significantly more detailed than the Kojiki, which dates from 712. Together with the Man'yōshū, these early works describe the tale of Urashima Tarō, among other stories.

By the time of the tenth-century Kokinshū anthology, waka had become the standard term for short poems in the tanka form. Waka refers to poetry composed in Japanese, unlike kanshi. Earlier, the word covered a wider range of Japanese-language poems.

The 10th-century Tale of the Bamboo Cutter can be considered an early example of proto-science fiction. Its heroine Kaguya-hime is a princess from the Moon, sent to Earth for safety during a celestial war and raised by a bamboo cutter. She is later taken back to her extraterrestrial family in a disc-shaped flying object.

The 10th-century Japanese narrative The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter may also be considered proto-science fiction. Its heroine, Kaguya-hime, is a princess from the Moon sent to Earth during a celestial war, and a manuscript illustration depicts a round flying machine similar to a flying saucer.
tags: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter

literature.text: The Samguk yusa contains 14 hyangga poems, and the Gyunyeojeon, a set of biographies of prominent monks, contains eleven. Both works were written much later, in the Goryeo dynasty. Yet the poems in the Samguk yusa appear to be based on no-longer-extant records from the Silla period.

science.text: Korea's Cheomseongdae is a 9.4-meter high astronomical observatory built in 634 CE. It is one of the best known artefacts of Korea's history of science and technology.

According to Nakayama Shigeru, nearly all 7th century astronomers in Japan came from Baekje. Native Japanese astronomers were gradually trained, and by the eighth century only forty percent of Japan's astronomers were Korean.

From the mid-fifth to the late-seventh centuries, Japan benefited from the immigration of people from Baekje and Gaya, known as Toraijin. Many of them were refugees who arrived during the intense regional warfare that racked the Korean peninsula. They brought knowledge of iron metallurgy, stoneware pottery, law, and Chinese writing.
The Ishinpō, a Japanese medical text written in 984, still contains many medical formulas of Korean origin. It shows how long Korean knowledge continued to shape Japanese medicine.

Japanese farmers divided their arable land using a system of measurement devised in Korea. It is one example of Korean influence on Japanese technology, since the peninsula was a cultural bridge between Japan and China.

politics.text: In 668 AD, the Korean kingdom of Silla conquered Baekje and Goguryeo with the aid of China's Tang dynasty, forming Unified Silla. In the north, Balhae succeeded Goguryeo.

Goryeo was founded in 918, during the Later Three Kingdoms period of national division. Kung Ye, the ruler of Taebong, was unstable and cruel: he proclaimed himself the Maitreya Buddha, claimed to read minds, and out of paranoia executed numerous subordinates and family members. His own generals deposed him in 918 and raised General Wang Kŏn to the throne, and Goryeo went on to unify the Korean Peninsula.

Between the 4th and 9th centuries, Japan's many kingdoms and tribes were gradually unified under a centralized government, nominally controlled by the Emperor of Japan. The imperial dynasty established at this time continues to this day, though in an almost entirely ceremonial role.

Korean historians call Goryeo's achievement a "true national unification". It unified the Later Three Kingdoms and also incorporated much of the ruling class of the northern kingdom of Balhae, who had origins in Goguryeo. The name Korea is derived from the name of Goryeo.

Beginning in the late 8th century, Later Silla was undermined by political turbulence in the capital and by class rigidity in the bone-rank system. The central government weakened, and regional lords called the hojok rose to power.

The military officer Kyŏn Hwŏn revived Baekje in 892 with descendants of Baekje refugees. In 901 the Buddhist monk Kung Ye revived Goguryeo with descendants of Goguryeo refugees. These two states, together with Later Silla, formed the Later Three Kingdoms.

The Taika Reform in the mid-7th century advanced Japan's political centralization. The greatest catalyst, however, was the devastating defeat by Tang China at the Battle of Baekgang in the latter half of the 7th century. In response, domestic powers reached a consensus to build a national system, and centralized power consolidated rapidly.

Later Silla was initially a period of peace, without a single foreign invasion for 200 years. It engaged in international trade from as distant as the Middle East and maintained maritime leadership in East Asia.

Later Silla followed a national policy of integrating Baekje and Goguryeo refugees, called the "Unification of the Samhan". Even so, the refugees kept their own collective consciousnesses and a deep-seated resentment and hostility toward Silla.

In 710, the Japanese government built a grandiose new capital at Heijō-kyō (modern Nara), modeled on Chang'an, the capital of Tang China. In this period the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki appeared, describing the imperial line as descendants of the gods.

Japan's capital moved briefly to Nagaoka-kyō in 784, then to Heian-kyō (modern Kyoto) in 794. Political power within the court soon passed to the Fujiwara clan, court nobles who grew increasingly close to the imperial family through intermarriage.

After Goguryeo's fall, the rest of its people established Balhae, which the article says won the war against Tang in the later 7th century. The Tang emperor admitted Balhae as 'a strong country in the East'. Balhae traded with Japan, China and Silla, until the Liao dynasty invaded it in the early 10th century and Balhae fell.

To form its new central army, the Ku-sŏdang, Later Silla divided it into 3 units of Silla people, 3 of Goguryeo people, 2 of Baekje people and 1 of Mohe people. The army thus deliberately mixed the peoples of the conquered kingdoms.

philosophy.text: In ancient Japan, the arrival of Buddhism was closely tied to the national construction and the centralization of power. Prince Shōtoku and the Soga family fought and overcame the Mononobe family, who had handled the ancient Japanese religion. They then drew up a plan for governing the nation based on unifying the legal codes and Buddhism.

Early Japanese rulers held that national peace and security came through the power of Buddhism. This idea is called the "making a country safe" thought. Nara Buddhism followed only this thought, in contrast to the later Buddhism of the Heian period.

Heian Buddhism promised more than national peace and security. It also offered personal worldly profit. Its practitioners often performed severe ascetic practices, incantations and prayers in the mountains, so this Buddhism came to be called mikkyō.

Buddhism entered Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread rapidly. Religious syncretization made kami worship and Buddhism functionally inseparable, a process called shinbutsu-shūgō. Native Japanese religion and the imported faith became deeply intertwined.

Prince Shōtoku served as regent of Empress Suiko and showed a deep understanding of the "foreign" Buddhism. He planned to stabilize national politics through its use. His approach laid the groundwork for the idea that Buddhism could keep the country safe.

In the Nara period, especially under Emperor Shōmu, Kokubun-ji and Kokubun-ni-ji temples were erected throughout the whole country. Tōdai-ji Temple and the Daibutsu were built in Nara. Buddhism had become a project of the state.

Kūkai, a Buddhist monk, learned Chinese esoteric Buddhism while on a diplomatic mission to the Chinese court. He combined Japanese Buddhism with those esoteric practices to form Japanese Shingon Buddhism.
Saichō, a Buddhist monk who also journeyed to China, learned the practices of the Chinese Tendai sect. He argued that the teachings of the Lotus Sutra should be the core of Japanese Buddhism.

In the Heian period, two prominent forms of Buddhism developed: Tendai, a Mahayana school derived from Chinese Tiantai, and Shingon, a Vajrayana school derived from Chinese Esoteric Buddhism. The centre of Japanese Buddhism was Mount Hiei near the old capital of Kyoto.
State support for Buddhism reached its apex in the Nara period. Jianzhen of the Tang dynasty brought an imperial ordination platform to Todai-ji Temple, which is cited as evidence of this peak.
As Buddhism and kami worship merged, the kami came to be viewed as part of Buddhist cosmology. They were also increasingly depicted anthropomorphically, in human form.
The earliest written tradition about kami worship was recorded in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Before these texts, kami veneration had been traced back to the Yayoi period.

culture.text: In 538 AD, Buddhism reached Japan through the Korean kingdom of Baekje. The new faith did not replace native Shinto. The two coexisted, a blending known today as Shinbutsu-shūgō, and the period is named Asuka after the de facto imperial capital.

From the mid-fifth to the late-seventh centuries, people from Baekje and Gaya immigrated to Japan. They were known as Toraijin, and many were refugees from the intense regional warfare that racked the Korean peninsula. They brought knowledge of iron metallurgy, stoneware pottery, law, and Chinese writing.

Shinto revolves around supernatural entities called kami, who are believed to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent landscape locations. The earliest written tradition regarding kami worship was recorded in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

The Heian period began in 794, when a new imperial capital was established at Heian-kyō, modern Kyoto. It is considered a golden age of classical Japanese culture. Japanese religious life from then on was a mix of native Shinto practices and Buddhism.

Buddhism entered Japan at the end of the Kofun period, and it spread rapidly. Kami worship and Buddhism became functionally inseparable through a process called shinbutsu-shūgō. The kami came to be seen as part of Buddhist cosmology and were increasingly depicted anthropomorphically.

The kamado stove was a continental invention, modified by peninsular peoples before reaching Japan. By the seventh century it was in widespread use, and historian William Wayne Farris says it had a profound effect on daily life. Japanese people called it kara kamado, meaning Korean ovens.

The traditional Japanese kimono can be traced back to the 7th century. The Japanese Imperial Court and aristocracy then started to wear garments adapted from traditional Chinese clothing. Gofuku, a term for high-end silk kimonos, refers to the dress of the Go style, from the original Wu region.

Hiragana and katakana are phonetic syllabaries developed from simplified kanji, derived from man'yōgana. Hiragana emerged around the 9th century, and women used it informally while men used katakana formally. By the 10th century, both systems were common.

Buddhist monks also carried tea to Korea during the Tang era. Korean histories such as Samkuk-yusa and Samkuk-sagi indicate that Korean royals were drinking tea by the 7th century, mostly sourced from China.

According to Nakayama Shigeru, nearly all 7th century astronomers in Japan came from Baekje. By the eighth century, as local astronomers mastered the science, only forty percent of Japanese astronomers were Korean.

Starting from the sixth century, advanced stonecutting technology entered Japan from Korea. Japanese tomb construction began to change in favor of Korean models. Around this time the horizontal tomb chambers prevalent in Baekje began to be built in Japan.

In the Later Three Kingdoms period, satirical poems were composed in Korea. One of them was the Sanghwajeom, the Colored-eye people bakery. It tells of a Korean woman who goes to a Muslim bakery to buy some dumplings.

Between 812 and 814 CE, a smallpox epidemic killed almost half of the Japanese population. It struck during the Heian period, after the capital had moved to Heian-kyō in 794 and the Fujiwara clan had grown close to the imperial family through intermarriage.
